78: Everything starts with the place where the bar lives between events. We do not rent a storefront or a production space. We rent a storage unit with parking for the trailer, budgeted at {{alquiler_mes}} per month in the example case. A drive-up unit of about 200 sq ft (19 m²) holds the trailer or, if you prefer to park it elsewhere, the portable bar, glass racks, coolers, ice bins, smallwares and spare mixers on shelving. Look for a unit with a power outlet, easy trailer access at any hour, good lighting and a gate you control, because loading happens early on Saturday mornings and late on Sunday nights. Glassware is washed in racks at the unit's wash station and counted out and back in at every event, so breakage is a number on the event sheet and not a surprise. Before paying a deposit, ask the facility whether it allows a trailer, whether its insurance covers what you store inside (most do not, so list it on your equipment coverage), and how much notice it needs to end the lease. Keep the rent in mind when you quote: it is a fixed cost that does not shrink in January.
79: Own what travels and rent what does not. The core is one used bar trailer ({{inv_vehiculo}}) with its conversion ({{inv_adaptacion}}): a bar top, cabinets, a speed rail, ice bins, a hand sink, fresh and gray water tanks and LED lighting. The wrap and bar facade ({{inv_fachada}}) is what gets photographed, so it is money well spent. A portable bar ({{inv_barra_portatil}}) serves the second crew and ballrooms the trailer cannot enter, an inverter generator ({{inv_energia}}) keeps the lights and coolers running, and glassware, coolers and dispensers cost {{inv_cristaleria}}. Your own pickup is the tow vehicle. If you do not have one, a used pickup runs from $10,000 to $30,000, according to Check Cherry, and that is a line you must add to the startup costs. Tables, linens, tents and extra glassware come from party rental companies and are passed through in the quote.
80: Every event follows the same written timeline. About three weeks out, the host fills in a brief with date, venue, guest count, event length and drink preferences. Two weeks out, we visit the venue to check power, water, load-in route and where the bar will stand, and at the same time we send the host a shopping list of the bottles to buy. The day before, we buy mixers, garnishes and ice, and load the trailer. On the day, we arrive 60 to 120 minutes before the first guest, set up, test the lights and chill the glassware. Service runs four to five hours and ends with a last call. Then we break down, wash, count the glassware and leave the space as we found it. We plan one bartender for every 50 guests at a full bar.
81: Ice, garnish and glassware are where a mobile bar wins or loses its margin. We plan about 1.5 lb (0.68 kg) of ice per guest, a Kit estimate, and buy commercial bagged ice so we never fill a bin from a tap of unknown origin. Garnish is cut as late as the county allows, and we ask the health department whether cut fruit must be prepared in a permitted facility. For drinks, eventplanning.com suggests two drinks per guest in the first hour and one per hour after that, so we size cups and mixers on that curve. Every bar carries at least one mocktail, and we mark allergens on the drink menu sign, especially orgeat and coconut. Cups, napkins and straws are in the package. Glass comes back in racks and is counted.
82: We buy mixers, syrups and disposables from a short list of suppliers, with a backup for each, and we order garnish and ice the day before so nothing sits for a week. A fresh supply of lemons and limes is cheap; a missed delivery on a Saturday is not. Party rental companies supply tables, tents and extra glassware, and their delivery times are written into the event sheet. The trailer and the tow vehicle follow a calendar: tires, brakes, lights, bearings and the electrical system are checked every quarter and again before wedding season, with a monthly pre-trip checklist. Fuel, registration and repairs are in the budget, because a breakdown on a Saturday costs more than any repair.
85: The team is small, and each person has a clear job. The owner works as lead bartender and also sells: writing proposals, running tastings and leading the biggest events. A second-crew lead bartender, on part-time W-2 hours, runs the portable bar and the smaller events. Event bartenders are W-2 employees paid by the hour, scheduled per event. Barbacks and setup crew, also hourly W-2, load the trailer, haul ice, wash glassware and keep the bar stocked. As volume grows, the first additions are more event hours and a third crew lead, not more fixed salaries.
86: Labor costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1, including employer payroll taxes, which is {{personal_pct}} of sales. That figure covers the owner's pay, the part-time crew lead and the hourly event bartenders and barbacks the workbook schedules for the year-1 volume. About a third of it, the hourly event bartenders and barbacks, moves with the calendar; your own pay and the crew lead's are fixed. We keep the owner's pay inside the number so the plan shows the real cost of running the business. You can test any change in pay or headcount directly on the "Staffing" tab of the workbook.
87: Event labor is the cost that moves with the calendar. Each event needs about {{horas_evento}} hours per person, counting prep, loading, travel, setup, service and breakdown, and an average of {{personas_evento}} people. The workbook spreads payroll evenly over the 12 months, which is conservative: in a quiet month you will pay fewer event hours. The workbook compares the hours scheduled with the hours needed and reports {{cobertura_horas}} coverage. As a Kit estimate, a full bar needs one bartender for every 50 guests, while a beer and wine bar stretches to one for every 75. We set staffing from the package we quote, never from habit, and we write the number of bartenders into the proposal.
88: We hire event bartenders and barbacks as W-2 employees. They work under our direction, on our schedule, with our equipment, which is the profile the Fair Labor Standards Act treats as employment, and California's "ABC test" for employment status (AB5) presumes it. Calling them independent contractors may look cheaper, but misclassification can bring back taxes, penalties and claims, and it can sink a loan application. Payroll taxes add {{cargas_pct}} to wages in the model, and workers' compensation is required in nearly every state. We pay at least the highest of the federal, state and local minimum wage; the workbook sets pay against a federal floor of {{salario_minimo_federal}} for full-time work, so check your city, as many are higher. For reference, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that bartenders earned a mean of $19.61 an hour and a median of $16.51 in May 2025, with tips included.
89: Training is part of the plan, not an extra. Everyone who pours holds an alcohol server certification: TABC in Texas, RBS in California, or TIPS and ServSafe Alcohol where the state has no program of its own. Venues and insurers often ask for the certificates, and in Texas the employer's safe harbor protects you when your staff is certified. Before the first event of the season, we run a short session on responsible service: checking ID, refusing minors, spotting a guest who has had enough, cutting off politely and calling last call. Each bartender also learns the specs of our signature cocktails, how to batch ahead without losing quality, and how to answer questions about allergens. Certificates are filed and checked at renewal. The workbook carries these courses on their own line.
90: Treat the service charge and the gratuity as two different things, because the IRS does. Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, a mandatory service charge is not a tip: whatever part you pay out to staff is wages, with payroll taxes. A tip is voluntary, and under the FLSA it belongs to the staff, not to the owner. We show the service charge and any voluntary gratuity on separate lines of the quote and say what each pays for. Tips need one more check. Missouri's circular lists tips, gratuities and donations among the payments that can count as a sale of alcohol, so ask your state ABC before you put out a tip jar or add a gratuity line; where in doubt, build the staff's pay into your service price.
93: The example describes a viable small business, not a guarantee. Year-1 revenue reaches {{ventas_a1}} with a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}, and EBITDA comes to {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales. Average revenue is {{ventas_evento}} per event, well above the $750 median that Check Cherry reports, so the case sits in the upper quarter of the market: a full-time operator with two crews, the trailer, mixers and ice included. Change the numbers on the "0. Assumptions" tab until they match your area.
94: Startup costs are built from lines you can price today. The used bar trailer costs {{inv_vehiculo}} and its conversion {{inv_adaptacion}}. The wrap and bar facade add {{inv_fachada}}, the portable bar {{inv_barra_portatil}}, the inverter generator {{inv_energia}} and the glassware, coolers and dispensers {{inv_cristaleria}}. First-year permits and certifications cost {{inv_permisos}}, the website, photos and first bridal show {{inv_lanzamiento}}, and the opening inventory of mixers, syrups, garnishes and cups {{inv_stock}}. There is no alcohol to buy, because the host pays for it. With the remaining lines, capex totals {{capex}}. A working capital reserve of {{fondo_maniobra}} brings the total investment to {{inversion_total}}. The owner contributes {{fondos_propios}}, and a loan of {{prestamo}} covers the rest, at {{tipo_prestamo}} nominal interest over {{plazo_prestamo}} years. The plan is lender-ready, but approval is never guaranteed.
95: Revenue grows with the number of events, not with price. The example moves from {{ventas_a1}} in year 1 to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3, because events per year grow by {{crecimiento_a2}} and {{crecimiento_a3}} while the price per guest and the guest count stay the same. Net profit follows at {{resultado_neto_a1}}, {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}, after loan interest, depreciation and income tax at an effective rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}}. That rate stands in for the income tax on the profit; if your LLC is a pass-through, the owner pays it personally, so keep the reserve anyway.
96: Direct costs are small because the host buys the alcohol. Mixers, garnishes and ice cost {{coste_paquetes_pct}} of bar package sales, and total cost of goods is {{cogs_pct}} of sales. Disposables, meaning cups, napkins and straws, are {{consumibles_pct}}, and card fees {{tarjeta_pct}}. Labor is {{personal_pct}} of sales, and the storage unit and trailer parking {{ocupacion_pct}}. The thresholds in the workbook are editable estimates, so adjust them to your market.
97: Break-even is measured in events per year. The business covers its accounting costs at {{equilibrio_eventos}} events and its cash costs at {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}} events, against {{eventos_a1}} in the plan (the workbook shows the exact figure; the plan rounds it up to whole events). The plan sits {{holgura_caja_pct}} above cash break-even, so events could fall by about {{caida_absorbible_pct}} before cash stops covering costs. Compare that with the market: the typical new mobile bar does far fewer.
98: Cash is the tight spot. The lowest balance in year 1 is {{saldo_minimo}}, reached in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}. Project payback before debt is {{payback}}, and the lowest DSCR over the loan term is {{dscr_min}}, against a lender guideline of {{dscr_objetivo}}. The model does not count the 30% deposit, so the real cash position is usually better.
99: Three scenarios show how fast the numbers move. The pessimistic case assumes {{pesimista_eventos}} events at {{pesimista_precio}} per guest and {{pesimista_invitados}} guests per event, which gives revenue of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}. Estimated year-1 closing cash is {{pesimista_caja}}: the cash runs out. That is the honest warning of the plan, because the median mobile bar in its first year does 3 events. The optimistic case reaches {{optimista_ventas}}. Start smaller, or keep more savings in reserve.
102: Dry hire is the legal model of this kit: the host buys the alcohol, and we sell the service. Missouri's Industry Circular 24-01 (atc.dps.mo.gov) says a person who solely provides bartending services does not need a state liquor license, and warns that admission, tips, gratuities, donations and surcharges on alcohol can count as a sale. The conditions are simple. The host buys and owns the alcohol, and leftovers go back to the host. Do not buy the alcohol for the host and get paid back: in Missouri, money for alcohol or its delivery can count as a sale, and Montana requires the host to buy it separately. There is no cash bar, no drink tickets and no ticket that includes drinks. The invoice separates your service from any reimbursements.
103: Montana's Department of Revenue, in its Mobile Bars fact sheet, goes further: a mobile bar may not pre-stock, the host buys the alcohol separately, the events must be private, and guests cannot be charged for drinks. Other states have their own versions, and the only constant is that it varies by state. Before you take your first booking, ask your state alcohol authority (the ABC, TABC or its equivalent) how it treats a bartending service, and keep the answer in writing. A phone call or an email is enough, and it can save you a fine.
104: Full-service, where your business buys and sells the alcohol, is an option, not the case of this kit, and it varies by state. In Texas, a Caterer's Permit is an auxiliary to a Mixed Beverage Permit tied to a fixed address. In California, a private event with no admission, no charge per drink and the host's alcohol generally needs no state license (Bus. & Prof. Code §23399.1; confirm with the ABC), and the Type 58 caterer license is for on-sale licensees. In Florida, selling without a license is a crime, so a cash bar needs a licensed partner (a 13CT caterer). In New York, a Caterer's Alcohol Permit from the SLA is issued per event, so check with the SLA first. The routes are a licensed partner, your own license tied to a venue, or an event permit where one exists.
105: The health permit depends on your county. No rule is written specifically for mobile bars, so some counties apply the rules for mobile food vendors by analogy: a permit, an inspection of the unit, limits on cut garnish and rules for ice. Call your county health department before you build, and ask what it requires for ice, garnish and a hand sink. Use commercial bagged ice and put a hand sink in the trailer, which most inspectors want to see anyway. The example reserves {{inv_health_permit}} for the inspection, and you should replace it with the fee your county charges, or zero if it requires none. Keep the answer, because venues and insurers sometimes ask for it.
106: Sales tax can reach the service. California taxes a caterer's charges for serving food and beverages, even when the client supplies them (CDTFA), so bartending charges are generally taxable there. Elsewhere it depends on whether your state taxes the service, the bar rental and the glassware. The workbook applies {{sales_tax}} to the whole invoice, the conservative choice. Register for a sales tax permit with your state. A mandatory service charge is wages under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, and a voluntary gratuity goes on its own line and belongs to the staff.
107: On insurance, plan for general liability and a separate liquor liability policy, because general liability usually excludes alcohol; for a mobile bartender, general and liquor liability, bundled, start around $550 a year, according to insurancecanopy.com. Add commercial auto that covers the trailer, workers' compensation and equipment coverage. The example budgets {{seguros_anual}} per year. Venues ask for a COI naming them as additional insured, and the host's own liquor liability is the host's purchase. Staff are W-2 employees, with Form I-9, Form W-4, workers' compensation and the FLSA applying to tips; California's AB5 presumes employment. In Texas, certified bartenders give you the safe harbor under section 106.14.
108: The trailer gets its own title, registration and plates at your state DMV (rules for light trailers vary, so ask), and your auto policy must cover business use. If you operate in the UK, the rules differ. Every sale at a venue with a premises licence must be authorized by a personal licence holder (18 or over, APLH Level 2, granted by the council), but you do not need one to sell under a Temporary Event Notice. A TEN costs £21, covers fewer than 500 people for up to 168 hours, and you can give 5 a year, or 50 with a personal licence, at least 10 working days ahead (gov.uk). At a licensed venue you work under the venue's licence, and a ticket that includes drinks counts as a sale.
111: The plan holds together because of how it is built. In dry hire there is no alcohol inventory to carry and, in most states, no liquor license to buy, so the capital stays low and the risk stays bounded. Two demand engines balance each other: weddings fill the weekends of peak season, and companies and private hosts fill the weekdays and the winter. The bar trailer gives the brand something to be photographed and remembered for, and the specialty bars give planners a reason to recommend it. One caution, honestly: the example is the upper quarter of the market. A new mobile bar usually starts with far fewer events, so build the first year on your own bookings, not on the case.
112: Know the risks before you sign anything. Late cancellations are handled by a 30% deposit at signing and a written cancellation schedule, and no date is held without both. An intoxicated or underage guest is handled by certified bartenders, responsible service rules and liquor liability coverage. A breakdown of the trailer or the tow vehicle is covered by maintenance, a portable bar as backup and a relationship with a local rental company. Rain at an outdoor event is handled by a written plan B and a tent rental company. Broken glass is counted and charged by the contract. A shortage of bartenders on a Saturday is handled by a bench of trained W-2 staff. A change in state alcohol rules is handled by asking your ABC each year.
113: Our strengths come from focus. We sell a small number of things well: a trailer that gets photographed, a short list of signature cocktails and specialty bars that justify a better price. We keep our risk low by not holding alcohol or a license, and our fixed costs low with a storage unit and a single trailer. Two crews let us serve two events on the same Saturday. Our dry hire service agreement is clean, with the service separated from the host's purchases. And we run on documented procedures, so quality does not depend on one heroic weekend.
114: The roadmap follows the six phases of the checklist in this kit. In "Phase 1 - Business Setup" you form the LLC, get your EIN, open the bank account and register for the sales tax permit. "Phase 2 - Trailer & Permits" covers the bar trailer, your state alcohol answer, the health permit and your insurance. "Phase 3 - Equipment" buys the glassware, coolers, bar tools and generator. "Phase 4 - Staff" sets up payroll, certifications and your bartender pool. "Phase 5 - Marketing" builds the website, your listings on The Knot, WeddingWire and GigSalad and your first tastings. "Phase 6 - First 90 Days" runs your first events and reviews each one afterward. Do not move to the next phase while permits from the current one are still open.
115: Measure a few things every week, and do not wait for the accountant. Track events booked per month against the plan's {{eventos_a1}} a year, and the share of proposals that become signed contracts. Track the average price per guest against {{precio_invitado}}, cost per guest for mixers, garnish and ice, and labor against {{horas_evento}} hours and {{personas_evento}} people per event. Track cancellations, the number of reviews collected after each event and repeat companies. If two or three of these drift for a month, fix them before you add events or buy a second trailer. For the first six months, review the list every Monday and write down one change.
116: Looking three years ahead, the plan grows from {{eventos_a1}} events to {{eventos_a3}} by building the repeat base of companies, which fills the weekdays and lowers the cost of selling each event. A third crew or a second trailer makes sense when the Saturday calendar and the cash balance both support it, and not before. Your own liquor license is a later decision, taken only if the numbers and your state allow it, since it brings dram shop liability and a fixed address. Each step is paid from cash flow, so the business does not depend on bigger loans.
117: The next steps are simple and in order. Open the Excel workbook and replace the example assumptions with your own events, price per guest and guest count. Use the pricing calculator to turn that into quotes you can send, with the shopping list for the host and the service charge and gratuity on separate lines. Then work through the startup checklist one phase at a time. This plan is a planning tool, not legal or tax advice. Check with your state ABC and your county, and with your accountant and attorney, before you commit money.
